paragraphs.mainIdea: They ran through the rain and mud to the tree house.

paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie would try first and read later.

paragraphs.context: • There was a time when many people
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Irish name for fairies is Sí, said like Shee.
paragraphs.simple: Long ago, many Irish people believed that fairies lived inside small hills. In Irish, fairies are called Sí, and you say it like "Shee". The writer uses "Shee" in the story.

paragraphs.context: • Leprechauns are a type of male Irish
paragraphs.mainIdea: Leprechauns are male Irish fairies who make shoes and hide gold.
paragraphs.simple: In old stories, leprechauns are men fairies. They often make shoes or clothes and hide pots of gold. People see them a lot on St. Patrick's Day, an Irish holiday on March 17.

background.note: A holiday on March 17 for Saint Patrick, who is very important in Ireland. People often wear green.

paragraphs.context: • When she was a child, Lady Gregory’s
paragraphs.mainIdea: Augusta's full name was Isabella Augusta Persse; she became Lady Gregory.
paragraphs.simple: As a child she was called Augusta. When she grew up, she married Sir William Gregory, a knight, so people called her Lady Gregory.

paragraphs.context: • Ireland’s most famous poet is William Butler
paragraphs.mainIdea: Her friend W. B. Yeats was a famous poet; they started the Abbey Theatre.
paragraphs.simple: William Butler Yeats is Ireland's most famous poet. He and Lady Gregory were good friends and started the Abbey Theatre in Dublin in 1904.

background.note: A great Irish poet (1865-1939). He won the Nobel Prize in 1923.
The capital city of Ireland.

paragraphs.context: • William Butler Yeats often accompanied Lady Gregory
paragraphs.mainIdea: Lady Gregory remembered the exact words of storytellers.
paragraphs.simple: Yeats often went with Lady Gregory to collect old Irish stories in country homes. She was very good at remembering exactly what the storytellers said. Writers say she made people value the stories of Irish country people.

paragraphs.context: • From the 1600s to the early 1900s,
paragraphs.mainIdea: English replaced the Irish language, but later Irish became important again.
paragraphs.simple: For about 300 years, people in many parts of Ireland stopped speaking Irish and spoke English. Later, when Ireland fought to be free, people wanted to learn Irish again. Since 1922 it has been an official language, and children learn it at school.

background.note: The old Celtic language of Ireland, also called Irish.
